newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba grants authorization for 40 foreign priests, nuns.
newsitem.headline: Cuba grants authorization for 40 foreign priests, nuns.

text.p: Cuba, following up rapidly on a first meeting between President Fidel Castro and Pope John Paul II, has authorised about 40 foreign Roman Catholic priests and nuns to come to work on the island, church sources said on Sunday.

The move grants permission to the largest single batch of foreign priests and nuns to come to the island in three decades, and halves a current waiting list of about 80 priests and nuns seeking approval to come to Cuba, the sources said.
It follows the meeting between Castro and the pope last Tuesday at the Vatican, at which it was agreed the pontiff will visit Cuba next year.

The authorisations, communicated to the church by Cuban authorities on Friday, are significant because delays allowing foreign priests and nuns to work on the island are a specific problem that Vatican authorities have said they would like to see resolved as church-state relations improve.

The church sources said the group approved included 15 priests and more than 20 nuns, mostly from Colombia, Mexico, Argentina and Spain. The group also included one priest who was born in Cuba, left the island as a child and who has waited some 20 years to be able to return to work in his native land as a priest.

The list of those approved included six people who were authorised immediately following the visit of the Vatican's Foreign Minister Jean-Louis Tauran to Cuba last month -- a trip that paved the way for last Tuesday's meeting at the Vatican.

During his visit Tauran specifically mentioned more rapid approval of visas for foreign priests and nuns as something the church would like to see. He also said that the church should enjoy a wider public space, including access to the media and a broader field of work for the church charity Caritas.

The authorisations appear to indicate a willingness by Cuban authorities to make some concessions as they seek improved relations with both the local church and the Vatican, and prepare for the pope's visit.

In another example of this, the Communist Party daily Granma on Saturday reported on a statement earlier in the week by Cuba's Cardinal Jaime Ortega welcoming the meeting between Castro and the pope and the prospect of the papal visit. Statements by the Catholic bishops are usually not reported in the state-run media.

Castro himself was warmly enthusiastic about his 35-minute session with the pontiff. He said it was a "miracle" that such a meeting had taken place, lavished praise on the pope and said he would be treated like a "king" when he comes to Cuba.

During his visit to Cuba, Tauran said there was a need for more religious personnel, both Cuban and foreign, as the church was undergoing a renewal in Cuba. There are currently some 450 nuns and 250 priests on the island, about half of them foreign.
But church sources say that until recently policy on granting visas has been slow, with few permissions given other than to replace personnel who die or leave the country.
More than 100 priests were expelled from the country and religious schools were closed down in the early 1960s as Castro's communist revolution sought to put an atheist stamp on the country.
